did_you_know.text: This psalm opens with the heading “A psalm of David.” The heading links the psalm to David, but does not explicitly state when it was written or on what occasion.

The verse contains the phrase “Sit at my right hand”—sitting at someone’s right hand is an image of honor, authority, and closeness. The king’s enemies are later described as “a footstool for your feet,” meaning that they have been subdued by him.

The LORD sends “the scepter of your strength” from Zion. Here, the scepter symbolizes power and rule, and the king is commanded, “Rule in the midst of your enemies”—that is, rule even in a place where his enemies are present.

The verse describes the people as coming willingly and voluntarily on the day of the king’s battle. It also includes images of holiness, youth, and dew, some of whose precise meanings are difficult to interpret.
The LORD swears an oath and “will not change his mind,” meaning that he does not revoke it. This is followed by the declaration: “You are a priest forever, according to the order of Melchizedek.”

Melchizedek is also mentioned by name in Genesis 14 as the king of Salem and “priest of God Most High.” Psalm 110 uses his name to describe a priesthood with an eternal character, but it does not explain in detail the meaning of the phrase “according to the order of.”

The verse places the LORD “at your right hand” and presents him as the one who crushes kings on the day of his anger. Thus, the image from the first verse is reversed: not only does the king receive a position of honor, but the LORD himself acts beside him against his enemies.

The description of war becomes more intense: the LORD “will judge the nations,” “pile up the slain,” and “crush the heads.” These are biblical images of judgment, defeat, and military victory—not a description of a quiet political triumph.

At the end, someone is described as sitting or walking along the way while drinking from a stream; “therefore he will lift up his head.” Lifting the head symbolizes recovery, confidence, and victory after the struggle.
